props.title: Inferno

sections.content: **Inferno** (2016) continues Ron Howard's adaptation of Dan Brown's Robert Langdon series, following The Da Vinci Code (2006) and Angels & Demons (2009). Tom Hanks returns as the symbolist professor, this time battling amnesia while racing to prevent a billionaire's plot to release a plague. The film struggles to recapture the intrigue of its predecessors, trading the religious conspiracy elements for a more straightforward bioterrorism plot. Like National Treasure (2004), it attempts to blend historical puzzles with action sequences, but the urgency feels forced compared to the measured mystery of **The Da Vinci Code**.

sections.content: The film's Florence and Venice locations echo classic Italian-set thrillers like **Don't Look Now** (1973) and **The Italian Job** (1969), but Howard's direction lacks their atmospheric tension. The amnesia plot device recalls The Bourne Identity (2002), though without the same visceral impact. Felicity Jones joins as Dr. Sienna Brooks, but their partnership lacks the chemistry Hanks shared with Audrey Tautou in the original film.

Visually, **Inferno** attempts to represent Langdon's hallucinations through Dante-inspired imagery, reminiscent of the hellish visions in **What Dreams May Come** (1998). However, these sequences feel more like stylistic flourishes than essential narrative elements. The film's commentary on overpopulation and pandemic fears connects to themes explored more effectively in films like Contagion (2011) and **12 Monkeys** (1995). sections.content: The shift from religious mysteries to biological warfare marks a significant departure for the series. While **The Da Vinci Code** and **Angels & Demons** built tension through historical and religious revelations, **Inferno** relies more on conventional action sequences. This transformation mirrors similar genre shifts seen in franchises like **Mission: Impossible** (1996), which evolved from cerebral espionage to high-octane action. The film's approach to global conspiracy draws parallels to **Outbreak** (1995) and **World War Z** (2013), though without their pandemic intensity.
